Genetic testing for the frataxin gene is the reference standard test. C
Physical and occupational therapy are important, with selective use of orthotics, botulinum injections, and systemic muscle relaxants for spasticity.C
Riluzole probably improves ataxia symptoms at 12 months.B
Idebenone may prevent cardiomyopathy progression and 5-hydroxytryptophan may improve neurologic symptoms in selected patients, based on limited quality evidence. B

The disease is progressive, with its severity linked to certain allele defects. The end result is loss of mobility (typically within 10-15 years from onset) and eventual death from cardiorespiratory failure (typically within 20-30 years from onset). B

background.definition: Friedreich ataxia is the most frequent neurodegenerative autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia. It involves the central nervous system, peripheral nervous system, spinal cord, pancreas, and heart.

list.listitem: The prevalence of Friedreich ataxia is less than 1 in 100,000 based on a systematic review of prevalence studies.
Friedreich ataxia is the most common progressive hereditary neurodegenerative disease leading to ataxia.
Friedreich ataxia is caused by a mutation of the frataxin gene on chromosome 9q13. This leads to reduced levels of frataxin, which is involved in the production of iron sulfur clusters.
A total of 98% of patients have a GAA homozygous mutation.
One in 90 white people is a carrier of the Friedreich ataxia gene.
The mutated frataxin gene yields decreased expression of the mitochondrial protein frataxin, which is used for processing iron into the mitochondria.

The lower fraxatin levels in the mitochondrial inner membrane cause a decrease in iron-sulfur-dependent enzymes, so iron accumulations form in the heart, liver, spinal cord dentate nucleus, and fibroblasts. The destruction in the dorsal root ganglion and the degeneration of the posterior columns of the spinal cord lead to the specific symptomatic findings.
In the fibroblasts, the iron-sulfur complexes decrease the iron-regulation proteins. Superoxide dismutase is one of the upregulated enzymes that impairs defenses to oxidative stressors.
Greater GAA expansion length and earlier age of disease onset are associated with an increase in the severity of cardiac hypertrophy and neurologic progression.
Friedrich ataxia typically presents as ataxia in patients aged 5 to 15 years; other symptoms include hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and impaired glucose intolerance or diabetes mellitus. C
Genetic testing for the frataxin gene is the reference standard test. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Ataxia and areflexi, but demyelination rather than axonal neuropathy
Ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, and hearing loss; also abnormal EEG

list.listitem: The typical presentation is a patient aged 5 to 15 years with progressive ataxia of limbs. There is loss of deep tendon reflexes in the lower limbs, but positive Babinski sign, and loss of vibratory sensation and proprioception in the lower limbs. Patients may also have cerebeller dysarthria (speech difficulty) and pyramidal signs.
On examination, there may be scoliosis and foot deformities (eg, hammertoes or pes cavus from weak intrinsic foot muscles). Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due to iron deposits is common (90%).
Diabetes mellitus from neurodegeneration of the pancreatic beta cells occurs in approximately 10% of patients.

Clinical criteria for possible Friedreich ataxia include sporadic or recessive progressive ataxia with either (1) lower limb areflexia and dysarthria, positive Babinski sign, or electrocardiograph (ECG) repolarization abnormalities, or (2) retained lower limb reflexes and ECG repolarization abnormalities. These are 95% sensitive with an 88% positive predictive value.

Harding's criteria for probable Friedreich ataxia are 63% sensitive with 96% to 98% positive predictive value. Essential elements include onset before age 25 years, progressive ataxia of gait and limbs, absent knee and ankle jerks, axonal picture on neurophysiology, and dysarthria after 5 years of onset.
Common oculomotor and vestibular findings include saccadic intrusions, impaired eccentric gaze-holding, angular vestibulo-ocular reflex deficits, and abnormal pursuit.

A polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test for GAA triplet repeat expansion in the frataxin gene is the recommended test to confirm the diagnosis of Friedreich ataxia. It is more accurate than the standard Southern blot analysis at identifying and noncarriers.
For most patients presenting with ataxia, order magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to look for brain and spine atrophy, and an electromyograph (EMG) to look for sensory and axonal motor neuropathy.
If patients have cardiovascular symptoms, order an ECG to assess for arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy, an echocardiogram for cardiomyopathy, and use a Holter monitor to look for suspected arrhythmia.
Test the fasting blood sugar level; if elevated, evaluate for diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance.
For young patients presenting with ataxia, consider EMG, MRI, and GAA expansion frataxin gene testing.
For patients with symptoms of cardiac involvement, order an ECG, Holter monitor, and an echocardiogram.
If blood sugar level is elevated, evaluate for diabetes mellitus and impaired glucose tolerance.
The most common alternate diagnosis is ataxia telangiectasia. Once diagnosed, the Friedreich ataxia rating scale can be used to monitor disease progression.

A small randomized trial of riluzole found a significantly greater likelihood of improvement in the Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia score. This is the only drug endorsed by the 2018 AAN guideline as effective.B

A systematic review found that 5-hydroxytryptophan may improve neurological symptoms in patients who have olivopontocerebellar or cerebellar atrophy; idebenone was effective for halting and reversing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy but did not improve neurological outcomes. Overall, clinical trial evidence is very limited.B
Coenzyme Q10, vitamin E, and iron chelation are often used but there is no evidence for their effectiveness.B
Treat secondary conditions (ie, heart failure, cardiomyopathy, and diabetes) with standard medications.

A practice parameter of the American Academy of Neurology found evidence of benefit for riluzole 100 mg per day, and insufficient evidence for a long list of medications including idebenone. It concluded that deferiprone may worsen symptoms of ataxia at 6 months.

A small trial of riluzole, used to treat ALS found benefit, but only had 55 patients. Those in the rilizole group were more likely to have an improvement in the Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia score (50% vs 11%, p = 0.002).

An evidence-based international guideline for management of Friedreich ataxia recommends local botulinum toxin injections for treatment of spasticity if it is severe and the benefits and harms are carefully weighed, and non-drug measures are no longer effective. They conditionally recommend baclofen tizanidine, gabapentin, and other similar medications for treatment of generalized spasticity and spasms. Drug therapies are not recommended for treatment of dysarthria.

A Cochrane review identified only 2 small RCTs of anti-oxidants (idebenone and a combination of CoQ10 and vitamin E) and found inadequate evidence to support or refute their efficacy. A larger unpublished studies of idebenone did not find any neurologic or clinical cardiovascular benefits.

An earlier, less rigorous review of 25 studies found that 5-hydroxytryptophan was better than placebo at improving neurological symptoms in patients who have olivopontocerebellar or cerebellar atrophy. Idebenone was more effective than placebo for halting and reversing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy associated with Friedreich ataxia. They also evaluated amantadine, phystigmine, L-carntitine, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, bigabatrin, phophatidylcholine, acetazolamide, 4-aminopyridaine, buspirone, coenzyme Q10, and vitamin E but found no evidence of effectiveness.

An trial randomized 103 patients to omaveloxolone or placebo, and based on per protocol analysis of 82 patients it improved a 99 point modified Friedreich Ataxia Rating Scale by 2.4 points more than placebo. While statistically significant, this difference is unlikely to be clinically significant.
Interferon gamma 1b was not effective in a randomized trial with 92 subjects.

New studies are being done on a class of drugs called pimelic diphenylamide histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors. They target the cellular level and silence the Friedreich ataxia gene during transcription.

Chelation therapy is often recommended for cardiomyopathy associated with secondary iron overload due to Friedreich ataxia, but there is no evidence of net clinical benefit. Deferoxamine, deferiprone, and deferasirox are the chelating agents most often used.
Etravirine has been identified as a potential drug but has not been evaluated to date in clinical trials.
Neuropathy: a consensus guideline recommends treating neuropathic pain with gabapentin, pregabalin, lamotrigine, amitriptyline, or duloxetine.
Spasticity and spasms: if non-pharmacologic means are not effective, a consensus guideline recommends drugs such as baclofen, tizanidine, benzodiazepines, dantrolene, gabapentin, or botox injections.

Heart failure: Diuretics for fluid overload, ACE or ARB, and beta-blocker (in adults). Consider spirinolactone if Stage 3 or 4, and avoid calcium channel blocers. Consider an implantable cardioverter defibrillator if LVEF <35% and NYHA functional class 2 or 3 despite optimal medical therapy, and expectation of at least 1 year's survival.
Surgery may be needed for symptomatic treatment of scoliosis and pes cavus or hammertoe defects.

Many patients use over-the-counter antioxidants such as vitamin E or coenzyme Q10 on the theoretical basis that Friedreich ataxia is in part due to a superoxide dismutase. Clinical trial data are lacking.

An evidence-based guideline for management of Friedreich ataxia recommends intensive upper limb rehabilitation, it conditionally recommends splinting or orthoses for spacticity, spasm or contracture, and contionally recommends electrical stimulation for upper limb symptoms. Custom ankle orthotics are recommended when ankle joint kinematics significantly impair gate. For patients who are no longer ambulatory, standing and sitting balance exercises are recommended. Limb strengthening is conditionally recommended. For treatment of dysphagia, there is no clear evidence for modified diets or thickened fluids, and the guideline panel recommended against electrical stimulation for treatment of dysphagia.

A consensus management guideline recommends physical and occupational therapy for treatment of the ataxia and weakness, protective footwear for patients with neuropathy, and ankle orthotics if needed to improve mobility in patients with spasticity.

Physical therapy may be helpful to preserve muscle strength. A study in patients with spinocerebellar ataxia, a closely related disorder, had improved leg muscle coordination after participating in a cycling regimen.
Consider occupational therapy to aid in the modification of activities of daily living, as needed.

A systematic review identified 7 RCTs with 203 patients evaluating the effectiveness of non-invasive electrostimulation. They found significant improvements in the Modified Ashworth Scale, cerebellar brain inhibition, the 8 meter walking time, the International Cooperative Ataxia Rating Scale, and the Scale for Assessment and Rating of Ataxia scores. Results were homogeneous, but the overall sample size is small.
A systematic review identified case reports for 47 patients undergoing mesenchymal stem cell therapy. While it appeared safe, no conclusions could be drawn regarding benefits.
Hospitalize for heart failure when appropriate.
The shorter allele GAA1 is the more severe the course.
The Friedreich ataxia rating scale is the most widely accepted and studied scale to monitor disease progression.
Friedreich ataxia is progressive and has a poor prognosis; within 10 to 15 years of onset (usually in the patient's late teens or 20s) the ability to sit, stand, and walk is lost.
Death typically occurs by the third or fourth decade of life from cardiopulmonary issues, with some variance depending on whether the patient has cardiomyopathy.

Late onset is in individuals older than 25 years; these patients have the same presentation and evaluation as classic patients, except they generally do not have pyramidal symptoms on examination and they will preserve the deep tendon reflexes.
Monitoring: ECG and echocardiogram annually.
